title: Handover: Byte, the Lab, Vanil and n8n
bridge: A handover is like fixing the bus factor on a component only one person understands. You record a walkthrough, write a runbook and add a second reviewer. Except watching is not owning. We count the handover as done only when the second person has shipped a real change through review.
intro: Four tools keep the platform alive today, and one person, Nave, can fix all of them. This lesson moves the Lab and Vanil into the RhinoHealth org and backs up n8n. It also makes a second maintainer able to fix Byte and the Lab. The proof is not a recording: the second maintainer ships a real change to each tool.

picture.caption: Two repos move into the org, n8n is backed up, and a second person learns to fix Byte and the Lab.

steps.text: transfers fcp-local-lab into the org; old clone URLs redirect
exports every workflow nightly as JSON (gitleaks before the first push)
a recorded 90-minute walkthrough of Byte, then one of the Lab
writes 'when it breaks' from the real failure modes
ships one small real change through normal review
fixes the page wherever reality differed

p: Open the telemetry branch of RhinoHealth/byte and read DASHBOARD.md. That branch holds no code, only Byte's run data: the dashboard and data/runs.jsonl, one line per review. The dashboard says: 411 reviews in the last 30 days, about $2.03 each. Byte reviews every agent PR. If Byte breaks tonight, only Nave can fix it.

The same is true for FCP Lab, which is the fcp-local-lab repo and the fcp-lab plugin. It is true for Vanil, the compliance sync built in n8n, and for n8n itself. Agents build and test inside FCP Lab on every full-size VM, so a broken Lab stops every agent run.

Four tickets fix this. G0-04 moves the Lab and Vanil into the org and backs up n8n. G0-05 and G0-06 hand Byte and the Lab to a second maintainer, each with a 'when it breaks' page. G0-17 makes that person ship a real change to each tool.

sections.h: Move the Lab and Vanil into the org (G0-04)
p: A second maintainer and the agents can only use what lives in the RhinoHealth org. fcp-local-lab lives in a personal account today, so confirm its current location with Nave. A repository transfer moves a repo to a new owner: in the repo, open Settings, then Transfer. GitHub redirects the old clone URLs, so nothing breaks on laptops.
Transfer it as a private repo and give it the same team access as fcp. Then point the fcp-lab plugin at the new URL. The plugin itself moves into RhinoHealth/claude-plugins in G8.

Vanil has no repo at all. Its two workflows, the hourly Vanta to Jira sync and the policy redline job, live only inside n8n's database. Export them as JSON into a new private repo, RhinoHealth/vanil. A workflow export holds credential names, not secret values, but run gitleaks on the JSON before the first push anyway.
gitleaks is a scanner that looks for keys and tokens in files and git history. Running it before the first push means a leaked value never reaches GitHub, where history is hard to clean.
The n8n database (RDS) already keeps 14 days of snapshots. What is missing is a readable copy of every workflow in git. Build the backup in n8n itself, as a workflow with three nodes.

A Schedule Trigger runs it nightly. The n8n node, with the operation Workflows: Get many, lists every workflow as JSON. The GitHub node, with create or edit a file, writes them into RhinoHealth/vanil. The GitHub token it uses is limited to that one repo.
Prove it the only way that counts: restore one workflow from the backup into a test n8n project and run it.

callout.text: A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup. The lab below makes you export, scan and read an export on your own laptop.

sections.h: The shape of a 'when it breaks' page
p: A 'when it breaks' page is a short runbook for the person who did not build the tool. It has three parts, in the order you use them at 2 a.m. First look: the three places to check, in order. Symptoms: a table of symptom, likely cause and fix. Escalate: who to call, and what the tool's failure costs.

The page comes from real failure modes, not from imagination. Where Nave does not know the fix yet, the page says so with a placeholder, and the walkthrough fills it in. Write it in the voice from lesson p12-4: plain, exact, one action per line.

Name the second maintainer from Platform before the session. Then Nave runs a recorded 90-minute walkthrough of RhinoHealth/byte. It covers the per-PR pipeline (gate, broker, review, sniff, finalize), fix mode, config/repositories.json, build-worker.yml signing, and the telemetry branch.

Afterwards the second maintainer gets write access to the byte repo, the #byte alerts, and approval rights on the worker-signing environment. The worker image is a signed image: the main build signs it, and the verify step refuses an image without that signature. The signing environment is where that signature is made, so the approval right matters.
sections.because: We write the page from Byte's real failure modes so the second maintainer can act before understanding everything.

code.text:
# When Byte breaks

Owner: Nave · Second maintainer: <name> · Alerts: #byte · Dashboard: DASHBOARD.md on the telemetry branch

## First look
1. The PR's "Byte Review" check and the caller run (byte-review.yml in the PR's repo).
2. The run artifact `byte-review-*`: the result JSON and the broker audit log.
3. `runner-canary.yml`: if the daily canary is red, the runner is the problem, not Byte.

## Symptoms
| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| No review after `@byte-review` | byte-runner-set at its max (15), or the gate skipped the PR | Look at queued jobs, then the gate log |
| Every run fails at the verify step | the main image was not signed (sign job red) | Rebuild from main; never repin by hand |
| Reviews behave like a branch build | shared `BYTE_WORKER_IMAGE` left on a branch digest | Restore the production digest |
| Every run fails at the model call | the Claude credential expired or was revoked | Rotate it as docs/setup.md says (by day 330) |
| Cost per review jumps | a prompt or playbook change, or re-review loops | Compare runs.jsonl week over week |

## Escalate
Nave, then the second maintainer. Byte is advisory: while it is down, PRs still merge with 1 approval.

notes.text: The header names the owner, the second maintainer, the alert channel and the dashboard. Replace <name>.
First look, step 1: the PR's 'Byte Review' check and the caller run. byte-review.yml is the thin caller in fcp.
Step 2: the run artifact holds the result JSON and the broker audit log, every call the worker made.
Step 3: runner-canary.yml runs daily. If it is red, the runner machines are broken, not Byte.
byte-runner-set is the pool of single-use runner pods Byte's jobs run on; its maximum is 15.
An unsigned image fails the verify step. Rebuild from main; never repin the digest by hand.
BYTE_WORKER_IMAGE is the shared variable that names the image digest. A branch test must restore it.
The Claude credential has a rotation date; docs/setup.md says how, by day 330.
runs.jsonl on the telemetry branch holds one line per run; compare weeks to find a cost jump.
Byte is advisory: it comments, it does not block. While it is down, PRs still merge with 1 approval.

p: After the transfer, Nave runs a second recorded walkthrough, this time of FCP Lab. It shows how lab-up boots cloud, client and frontend from a working tree, seeding, per-environment isolation, lab-doctor and lab-clean. The page's first look is those two commands and the failing service's logs.

This page has a second reader. G3's Packer image needs the Lab's images, the seed database and the compose files. List what G3 needs and who to ask. Then give the second maintainer write access and make them a reviewer on Lab PRs.
sections.because: The Lab runs on every full-size agent VM, so its page must work for a stranger on a VM too.

code.text:
# When FCP Lab breaks

Owner: Nave · Second maintainer: <name> · Runs on: laptops, and every full-size agent VM (G3)

## First look
1. `/fcp-lab:lab-doctor`: Docker engine, memory, architecture, and what already holds room.
2. `/fcp-lab:lab-clean`: what is running and what can be freed.
3. The failing service's logs in the stack's compose project.

## Symptoms
| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Stack never gets healthy | too little Docker memory, or another stack holds the ports | lab-doctor, then lab-clean the old stack |
| Seed step fails | migrations changed on the branch | <fill in from the walkthrough> |
| Image pull fails | Nexus or ECR login, or a missing image tag | <fill in from the walkthrough> |
| Works on a Mac, fails on an agent VM | arm64 vs. x86 images | <fill in from the walkthrough> |

## Escalate
Nave, then the second maintainer. On an agent VM, the run's health check (G3) stops the run
before any code is written, so a broken Lab costs time, not bad PRs.

notes.text: The Lab runs in two places: laptops, and every full-size agent VM from G3.
/fcp-lab:lab-doctor checks the Docker engine, memory, architecture and what already holds room.
/fcp-lab:lab-clean shows what is running and what can be freed.
Each stack is a compose project; the failing service's logs are the third place to look.
Two stacks on one machine fight over ports and memory: run doctor, then clean the old one.
A seed failure usually means the branch changed migrations. The fix is filled in from the walkthrough.
Images come from Nexus and ECR; a login problem or a missing tag stops the pull.
A Mac is arm64 and an agent VM is x86; an image built for one may not exist for the other.
On an agent VM, G3's health check stops the run before any code is written. A broken Lab costs time, not bad PRs.

sections.h: The second maintainer ships a change (G0-17)
p: A walkthrough is not a handover. In W3 the second maintainer picks, with Nave, one small real change in Byte and one in the Lab. Each is under half a day: a Byte ROADMAP.md item or open issue, and a Lab issue.

Byte: npm ci and npm run check, then try the change on a branch image as the README's Deploying section says. Restore BYTE_WORKER_IMAGE afterwards, merge, and watch the main build sign and repin the image.

Lab: make the change, boot a full stack with lab-up, run lab-review on the change, merge. Nave reviews but does not drive. Last, fix both 'when it breaks' pages wherever reality differed from the page.

callout.text: If the branch test ends with BYTE_WORKER_IMAGE still on the branch digest, every review behaves like a branch build. Restore the production digest; it is the third row of Byte's symptoms table.

lab.faded: Build the backup shape in your local n8n: a Schedule Trigger, then an n8n node with Workflows: Get many. The n8n node needs an API key, made under Settings, n8n API. The step left out is the GitHub node with a token limited to one repo. On the laptop, end the workflow with a node that writes the JSON to /home/node instead. lab.done: gitleaks prints no leaks found on the real export and leaks found: 1 on the planted file. Both of your pages have the three parts.

quiz.q: Vanil's workflow export is ready as JSON. What happens before the first push to RhinoHealth/vanil?

options.text: Push it; the repo is private and exports hold credential names, not values
options.why: Private is not safe: history is hard to clean, and a value can slip into a node parameter.

options.text: Run gitleaks on the JSON, then push
options.why: The ticket says so: exports should hold names only, and the scan proves it before anything reaches GitHub.

options.text: Delete every credential name from the JSON by hand, then push
options.why: Names are not secrets, and a restore needs them to find the right credential.

quiz.q: Byte is down for a whole day. What happens to pull requests in fcp?

options.text: Nothing merges until Byte is back
options.why: Byte is not a required check; it comments, it does not block.

options.text: Nave approves each PR by hand in Byte's place
options.why: No person stands in for Byte; the normal 1-approval rule already covers PRs.

options.text: PRs still merge with 1 approval; Byte is advisory
options.why: The Escalate line of Byte's page says exactly this.

quiz.q: Which of these proves the Byte handover is done?

options.text: The second maintainer has shipped one real change through review, with Nave reviewing, not driving
options.why: G0-17 is the proof: build, test, deploy and the page corrected where it was wrong.

options.text: The 90-minute walkthrough recording exists and the page is written
options.why: A walkthrough is not a handover; nobody has yet shown they can fix anything.

options.text: The second maintainer has write access, #byte alerts and signing approval
options.why: Access is a precondition, not proof; the change through review is the proof.
